title: Senses Are Weighted By Their Reliability

scenes.tts: You grip a bar and look at it. Your eyes say fifty millimetres. Your hand says fifty-four. These numbers are made up, but the question is not. A nervous system has to decide how much to trust each sense. Which one do you believe?
scenes.caption: You grip a bar and look at it. Your eyes say 50 mm. Your hand says 54. These numbers are made up, but the question is not. A nervous system has to decide how much to trust each sense. Which one do you believe?
scenes.visual: Axis of bar height; a blue marker at 50 and an orange marker at 54; a yellow question mark slides between them.
scenes.narration: You grip a bar and look at it. Your eyes say 50 mm. Your hand says 54. These numbers are made up, but the question is not. A nervous system has to decide how much to trust each sense. Which one do you believe?

scenes.tts: Each sense gives a noisy estimate. Suppose the noise in each is independent and Gaussian, the estimates are unbiased, and you have no prior preference for any height. Then the combination with the least variance is a weighted average. Each weight is the sense's precision, one over its variance, divided by the sum of the precisions.
scenes.caption: Each sense gives a noisy estimate. Suppose the noise in each is independent and Gaussian, the estimates are unbiased, and you have no prior preference for any height. Then the combination with the least variance is a weighted average. Each weight is the sense's precision, 1 over its variance, divided by the sum of the precisions.
scenes.visual: The markers grow into noisy bell curves; three lines build: weighted average, precision = 1 / variance, weight = precision / sum of precisions.
scenes.narration: Each sense gives a noisy estimate. Suppose the noise in each is independent and Gaussian, the estimates are unbiased, and you have no prior preference for any height. scenes.tts: Take vision with a standard deviation of two millimetres, and touch with four. Their variances are four and sixteen square millimetres. The weights come out at zero point eight for vision and zero point two for touch. The combined estimate is fifty point eight millimetres, much nearer to vision.
scenes.caption: Take vision with a standard deviation of 2 mm, and touch with 4. Their variances are 4 and 16 mm². The weights come out at 0.8 for vision and 0.2 for touch. The combined estimate is 50.8 mm, much nearer to vision.
scenes.visual: Legend rows gain SD and variance; a weight bar splits 0.8 blue / 0.2 orange; a green marker glides from 50 to 50.8.
scenes.narration: Take vision with a standard deviation of 2 mm, and touch with 4. Their variances are 4 and 16 mm². The weights come out at 0.8 for vision and 0.2 for touch. The combined estimate is 50.8 mm, much nearer to vision.

scenes.tts: The combined variance is three point two square millimetres. The standard deviation is about one point seven nine millimetres. That is lower than either sense alone. Touch is the weaker cue, yet it still makes the estimate more precise. Under these assumptions, a second independent cue always lowers the variance.
scenes.caption: The combined variance is 3.2 mm². The standard deviation is about 1.79 mm. That is lower than either sense alone. Touch is the weaker cue, yet it still makes the estimate more precise. Under these assumptions, a second independent cue always lowers the variance.
scenes.visual: A green combined curve grows narrower than both; SD comparison 1.789 < 2 < 4; touch curve pulses.
scenes.narration: The combined variance is 3.2 mm². The standard deviation is about 1.79 mm. That is lower than either sense alone. Touch is the weaker cue, yet it still makes the estimate more precise. Under these assumptions, a second independent cue always lowers the variance.

scenes.tts: Now blur the picture until vision has a standard deviation of eight millimetres. The weights swap: touch gets zero point eight, and vision zero point two. The estimate moves to fifty-three point two millimetres. The same arithmetic that favoured vision now favours touch. Alais and Burr found a related pattern for sound and sight in humans: when they blurred the visual stimulus severely, sound captured the perceived location.
scenes.caption: Now blur the picture until vision has a standard deviation of 8 mm. The weights swap: touch gets 0.8, and vision 0.2. The estimate moves to 53.2 mm. scenes.visual: The blue curve widens to SD 8, the weight bar flips, the green marker moves to 53.2; then a card shows a perceived-location marker pulled from a blurred sight band most of the way toward a sound line, labelled schematic, not data.

scenes.tts: Ernst and Banks tested this with four human observers, who judged bar height by sight and by touch while noise was added to the visual stimulus. A maximum likelihood model closely resembled their judgements. That is one task, four people, and a behavioural fit. It does not show where in the brain the weighting happens. Keep the rule: which sense wins follows its reliability in the task at hand.
